paras: The lynching of Benjamin Gorman took place in Webster County, Georgia, on the evening of Friday, May 29, 1903, when a crowd described as friends of Shelley Kent hanged Gorman, a Black man accused of killing Kent, a young white farmer, with a hoe the day before. According to the Dawson News, the crowd took Gorman from a bailiff who was trying to bring him to jail. An Associated Press dispatch carried the story widely, and Gorman's name later headed lists of June lynchings in white and Black papers.

Shelley Kent, whose name some papers spelled "Shelly," was a 21-year-old farmer who lived near Church Hill in Webster County, and the Americus Times-Recorder described him as "held in highest esteem." On Thursday, May 28, Kent and Gorman were at work together in a field when, according to the reports, the two had words. The Times-Recorder said the words concerned "some transaction between them," while the Dawson News traced the quarrel to fifteen cents that Gorman owed Kent. As Kent turned away, these accounts said, Gorman struck him on the head from behind with a hoe and crushed his skull, an attack the wire report called "without provocation." Gorman then fled.

Kent died of the blow, a few hours later by the Times-Recorder's account and on Friday according to the Savannah Morning News and the Dawson News. On Friday evening, the Times-Recorder wrote, "a number of the friends of the murdered man" went after Gorman and quickly captured him. The Dawson News added that after his capture Gorman was in the hands of Bailiff Marshall, who was trying to take him to jail, and that the crowd, "while orderly, was determined to Lynch him." The crowd took Gorman from the officer and hanged him from a tree.
The Times-Recorder placed the lynching "near Preston" and said it "was quietly conducted and no disorder ensued." Word of the lynching reached Americus on Saturday, May 30.
No report of an inquest, an arrest or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage, and no paper named any member of the crowd.

The Americus Times-Recorder printed the fullest account on May 31 under the headline "To Slayer of Kent No Mercy Is Given." Its story treated Gorman's guilt as settled, said that "justice" had been dealt him "at a rope's end," and concluded that "the murder of a good man was avenged." The Dawson News headlined its June 3 report "Fifteen Cents Cause Murder and Lynching" and opened with the stock phrase that "Judge Lynch had a session of his court in Webster county."

The Associated Press dispatch, dated Americus, May 30, ran on May 31 in the Savannah Morning News, the Montgomery Advertiser and the Richmond Times-Dispatch. It also ran in the Birmingham Age-Herald and, over the next two days, the Barre Daily Times in Vermont and the Wilmington Semi-Weekly Messenger. Its headlines named Gorman only by race and charge, as in "Negro Murderer Lynched" and "Another Georgia Lynching." Shorter versions drifted: the Newberry Herald and News of South Carolina placed Webster County in Alabama, and a weekly digest in the Olneyville Times and the Passaic City Record said Gorman "was taken from jail and lynched."

No narrative of the case appears in the Black press, which recorded it only in monthly tallies. On July 4 the Indianapolis Freeman printed a list of June lynchings beginning "June 1—Benjamin Gorman, colored, Webater county, Georgia," remarking that June had kept its reputation as "the month of fatalities." The Seattle Republican ran the same list on August 7. Nearly identical June lists, also dated June 1, appeared in white weeklies such as The Leader and the Osceola Times, and the Indianapolis Journal counted Gorman in its tally "Lynchings in 1903."

The reports differ on whether Gorman was in custody when he was killed. The Times-Recorder mentioned no officer, the weekly digest said he was taken from jail, and the Dawson News, a nearby Georgia paper, gave the most specific version, a seizure from a bailiff on the way to jail. The June 1 date in the lynching lists also differs from the Georgia papers, which put the lynching on Friday evening, May 29.

reader.title: Lynching of Benjamin Gorman
bases: Kent's friends or a crowd of 'enraged citizens' captured Gorman, took him from a bailiff and hanged him to a tree for the alleged murder of Kent (A1, A2, A11).

Gorman was hanged without any legal process by 'a number of the friends of the murdered man' (A1), described as a 'crowd' that took him from a bailiff (A11); the papers framed it as punishment for the alleged murder of Kent, 'justice thus having been dealt him' (A1) and a session of 'Judge Lynch' (A11).

The Americus Times-Recorder (A1), the AP dispatch from Americus (A2) and the Dawson News (A11) agree on the killing of Kent, the capture and the lynching on Friday evening; the Dawson News shares some AP wording but adds its own details on the debt and the bailiff.

accounts.label: Americus Times-Recorder (local)
accounts.gist: After words over 'some transaction', Gorman struck Kent from behind with a hoe; Kent died a few hours later; Kent's friends pursued and captured Gorman Friday evening and promptly lynched him near Preston, quietly.

accounts.label: Wire report from Americus
accounts.gist: Gorman killed Kent 'without provocation' in a field Thursday; after Kent died Friday, 'enraged citizens' captured and lynched Gorman that evening.

accounts.label: Dawson News
accounts.gist: The quarrel arose over fifteen cents Gorman owed Kent; after his capture Gorman was in the hands of Bailiff Marshall, who was taking him to jail, when an orderly but determined crowd took him and hanged him to a tree.

accounts.gist: Gorman was 'taken from jail and lynched' for the murder of Kent at Church Hill.

framing.detail: The Times-Recorder headlined 'To Slayer of Kent No Mercy Is Given', called the lynching 'justice' and said 'the murder of a good man was avenged'.
The Dawson News headlined 'Fifteen Cents Cause Murder and Lynching' and wrote that 'Judge Lynch had a session of his court', stressing the crowd was 'orderly'.
AP reprints ran under heads such as 'Negro Murderer Lynched' and 'Another Georgia Lynching', calling Kent's killing 'without provocation'.
The Freeman listed the case in its June tally, introduced with a remark that June had sustained its reputation as 'the month of fatalities'.
The Seattle Republican reprinted the June list without comment.
